title: Dynamic headroom allocator and ex-post burst reconciliation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Dedicated pools expose reserved throughput guarantees plus limited burst capacity. Current burst handling is static (fixed per-tenant leaky buckets) and produces edge cases: short hot-spikes consume disproportionate burst tokens, and post-facto SLA crediting is coarse-grained leading to customer confusion and manual reconciliations.

Goal: Implement a dynamic headroom allocator that: (1) proactively reserves small per-tenant headroom slices based on short-term demand forecasts, (2) allows overflow bursts to borrow against that headroom with fine-grained usage attribution, and (3) performs an ex-post reconciliation pass that issues SLA credits and corrects tenant balances using a transparent, auditable algorithm.

Scope: design, prototype, validation in staging, integration with ledger and billing job, rollout to canary pool. Not in scope: changing pricing tiers or legal contract language.

High-level approach:
- Sliding-headroom windows: maintain a moving 30s headroom budget per tenant derived from a combination of recent token rate, historical diurnal profile, and explicit reservation.
- Borrow and amortize: bursts first consume headroom (cheap), then borrow provisional credits from a cluster-level burst pool. Borrowed usage is tagged with request-level metadata so ex-post passes can attribute costs and SLA effect.
- Reconciliation engine: night-run job that replays sampled request logs + KV-cache state, computes expected throughput vs. reserved throughput under SLO, and emits ledger adjustments + SLA credits. Adjustments use per-token weighting to avoid punishing tenants for transient token surges caused by long responses.
- Telemetry & explainability: every adjustment emits an audit record with the causal chain (headroom used, burst borrow events, kernel-level preemptions) and a human-readable rationale for customer-facing credits.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Aggressiveness vs. predictability: larger headroom reduces rollbacks but increases potential oversubscription; we tuned toward conservative headroom to protect pool SLOs.
- Complexity vs. debuggability: adding demand forecasting increases accuracy but complicates audits; we limit forecasts to simple EWMA and retain raw logs for deterministic replay.
- Real-time vs. ex-post: real-time corrections reduce surprise to tenants but add complexity to serving path; we keep reconciliation ex-post to avoid latency risk and provide clear audit trails.

Acceptance criteria:
- Reconciliation accuracy: ledger adjustments for staged tenants align with ground-truth replay within 1% of billed tokens over 24h on noisy workloads.
- SLA handling: automated SLA credit issuance matched to manual analysis for at least 95% of test incidents.
- No measurable increase in median p50 latency on canary pool (<= 2% change) and no regression in p99 SLO targets.
- Auditability: every adjustment has a linkable audit record and an exportable CSV for billing review.

Rollout plan:
1) Design review and proto (this ticket) -> done.
2) Implement allocator and taggable burst borrow events (branch: feat/allocator/ENG-43888).
3) Staging validation via replay harness and fuzzed spike generator (2 weeks).
4) Nightly reconciliation job and ledger integration.
5) Canary: enable for 3 low-volume dedicated pools for 72h with human-in-the-loop review.
6) Progressive ramp to all dedicated pools with opt-out window.

Implementation notes and infra changes required:
- New per-tenant headroom table in the metering service (time-series eviction policy).
- Add borrow-event tagging to the serving runtime RPC envelope (request_metadata.burst_tag).
- Reconciliation service component that consumes S3 log slices and produces ledger writes via existing billing API.
- Dashboard panels in Console: headroom utilization, borrow rate, reconciliation-adjusted credits.

Open questions:
- Threshold for ex-post forgiveness on long-leading response generation where tokens are emitted slowly but tail latency contributes to headroom consumption. Recommendation: treat long responses as continuous token streams and amortize at per-second token rate.
- Edge behavior when pool-level burst pool is exhausted: should overflow route to compatible model variant (cheaper) or strictly throttle? Current guardrail: prefer graceful throttling with explicit customer events and a policy to offer fallback routing in a follow-up ticket.

References/Artifacts:
- Design notes: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DED/Billing+Headroom+Allocator
- Replay harness (proto): https://github.com/redwood-inference/billing-replay/pull/12
- Concept demo dashboard: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/allocator/proto

Expected follow-ups:
- PM doc to align contract language for SLA credits (PM: coordinate with legal).
- UX flows to notify tenants when reconciliations produce adjustments.
- ML ops exploration to test LSTM forecast vs. EWMA for headroom predictions (spike-only experiment).
